title: Minimum Necessary and Permissible Disclosures (TPO)

sections.learningObjectives:
- Explain the HIPAA minimum necessary standard and how it limits uses, disclosures, and requests of protected health information.
- Identify treatment, payment, and health care operations (TPO) uses and disclosures that are permitted without an individual's authorization.
- Recognize the exceptions to the minimum necessary standard, including treatment disclosures, disclosures to the individual, authorized disclosures, disclosures to HHS, and disclosures required by law.
- Apply role-based access, reasonable safeguards, and office policy to share only the information needed for a given task.
- Distinguish activities that require a valid authorization (such as marketing and psychotherapy notes) from those permitted under TPO.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of it like a locker room: you only take out the one item you actually need, not dump the whole locker. The minimum necessary rule says offices should share only the smallest amount of patient information needed to get a job done.

### Question 2

The rule covers three moves: using information inside the office, sharing it with someone outside, and asking another place to send you information. All three should use only what is needed.

### Question 3

It is like locking your bike with a good lock: you do something sensible to protect it, even though you cannot make it perfectly impossible to steal. Offices take sensible steps to protect information without making work impossible.

### Question 4

Imagine a school where the gym teacher can only open the gym supply closet, not the principal's office. Role-based access is the same idea: each worker gets a key only to the information they need.

### Question 5

If you do the same chore every day, you make a checklist once instead of deciding each time. Offices do the same: they write a standard list of what to send for common requests.

### Question 6

A cashier needs to know what you bought and how much it costs, not your whole life story. A billing clerk needs the billing details, not the private clinical notes.

### Question 7

If a stranger asks to see every kid's locker at school, the teacher does not open them—she goes to the principal. The assistant should also pause and ask the person in charge instead of sharing records.

### Question 8

For unusual requests, you cannot use a standard checklist, so you stop and think about exactly what is needed for that one case before sharing anything.

### Question 9

Even if your classmate's desk is open, you are not supposed to read their private notebook just because you are curious. The same rule protects patient charts.

### Question 10

If a trusted office says 'I only need these two pages,' it is fair to trust them and send those two pages, rather than double-checking their whole request every time.

### Question 11

When you borrow a book for a project, you take only the chapter you need, not the whole library. A referral should include just the information the specialist needs.

### Question 12

Privacy is not just about keeping secrets from outsiders; it also means coworkers should not peek at information that is not part of their job.

### Question 13

In a big shared building, each worker gets a keycard that opens only their own rooms. A shared computer system works the same way: each login opens only the screens that person needs.

### Question 14

You can tie your shoes carefully, but a lace might still come undone sometimes. The rule asks offices to be careful, not to be perfect at all times.

### Question 15

The school principal writes the rules and trains teachers; one person is in charge of making sure the rules are followed. The office does the same with a privacy officer and training.

### Question 16

If a store asks for your ID to process a return, they need your name and receipt, not your whole wallet. An insurer needs the billing details, not the entire medical chart.

### Question 17

If someone asks to borrow 'every single book in the school' for a vague reason, that is a red flag. Asking for one specific book for a clear reason is normal.

### Question 18

To check if a library card is valid, you need the person's name and card number, not a list of every book they ever borrowed.

### Question 19

PHI is any health information that points to a specific person, like a name plus a diagnosis, whether it is written, typed, or spoken.

### Question 20

You would not share a secret on a megaphone in a crowded room. The assistant should share patient information quietly and only with the right person.

### Question 21

When a patient moves to a new doctor, the old doctor sends the notes the new doctor needs to keep treating them, like passing the important pages of a notebook—not every old page.

### Question 22

If you erase every name and identifying detail from a test paper so no one can tell whose it is, it is no longer about a specific person—so the privacy rules do not apply to it anymore.

### Question 23

TPO is a short nickname for the three normal jobs a doctor's office does: treat people, get paid, and run the office properly.

### Question 24

A doctor's office can treat you, bill your insurance, and run its office without asking you to sign a special permission form every single time.

### Question 25

When doctors talk to each other to decide how to help a patient get better, that is treatment—working together on the patient's care.

### Question 26

Payment is everything about getting the bill paid—checking if insurance covers the visit and sending the claim to the insurance company.

### Question 27

Health care operations is about running the office well—checking quality, training workers, and reviewing how things are going—like a coach reviewing the team's performance.

### Question 28

When you get sent to a specialist, your regular doctor's office is allowed to send your information along so the specialist can help you—no special signed form is needed for that.

### Question 29

The office is allowed to send the bill to your insurance company so it can get paid—that is normal and does not need a special permission form.

### Question 30

Improving how the office works—like finding ways to shorten the wait—is allowed because it helps the office run better, and it does not need a signed form.

### Question 31

A doctor's office can share your information with another doctor who is helping take care of you, so everyone caring for you is on the same page.

### Question 32

One medical office can send billing information to another office or insurance company when that other place needs it to get paid.

### Question 33

One office can share information with another office to help that office run better, but only if they both have (or had) a connection to the patient and the information is about that connection.

### Question 34

When you switch to a new coach, your old coach sends over your practice notes so the new coach knows what you have been working on.

### Question 35

The normal work of treating you, billing for it, and running the office does not need a signed form—but most other ways of sharing your information do.

### Question 36

Sharing information to help another office run better is only okay when both offices have a link to the patient, and even then you share only what is needed.

### Question 37

Checking the office's own work to make sure bills and codes are right is allowed—like a teacher grading homework to see how the class is doing.

### Question 38

If you move to a new doctor, the old office can send your records to the new doctor so your care continues—no special signed form is needed for that transfer.

### Question 39

Talking with another doctor about what is wrong with a patient is treatment. Payment is about the money part, like billing and insurance.

### Question 40

If doctors had to ask for a signed form before every single step of your care, nothing would get done. The rule lets normal care and billing happen while still protecting your privacy.

### Question 41

When a medical supply company needs to confirm your order and insurance before shipping, the office shares just the details needed to complete the order—not your whole file.

### Question 42

The rule is like two clubs that can share a member's file only if that person actually belonged to both clubs, and the file is about their time at those clubs.

### Question 43

Before sharing your information with a helper company, the office checks that there is a signed agreement in place, then sends only what that helper needs to do the job.

### Question 44

Health care operations is the 'keeping the office running well' category—quality checks, staff training, and reviewing records to catch mistakes.

### Question 45

When a doctor shares information so another doctor can treat you, they do not have to stop and trim it down first—that sharing is exempt from the 'just the minimum' rule.

### Question 46

You are always allowed to see your own information. The 'only share the minimum' rule does not apply when you are asking about yourself.

### Question 47

If you give permission for something specific to be shared, the office can share exactly what you approved—it does not have to trim it down to a smaller amount first.

### Question 48

The government office that checks whether privacy rules are being followed can ask for records, and the office must provide them—this is not limited by the 'minimum' rule.

### Question 49

If a law says the office must send certain information, the office sends what the law requires—the 'just the minimum' rule does not apply to that.

### Question 50

When the government's privacy watchdogs come to check that the office is following the rules, the office must show them what they ask for.

### Question 51

Your own health information is yours to see. When you ask for it, the office gives you what you are entitled to see—the 'minimum' rule does not apply to you.

### Question 52

A signed permission form lets the office share exactly what the form describes. That sharing does not have to be trimmed down to a smaller amount.

### Question 53

The rule is a bit like a door that is locked for some people and open for others: it applies to billing, but it is open when the patient asks about themselves.

### Question 54

If a judge or the law says certain records must be handed over, the office follows that legal instruction—the 'minimum' rule steps aside for the law.

### Question 55

If another doctor is helping your doctor take care of you, the rules let them share what is needed to help you get better, without slowing things down.

### Question 56

Most normal care and billing does not need a signed form, but a patient's private therapy notes are extra-protected and usually need the patient's permission to share.

### Question 57

Your doctor's office cannot sell your name to advertisers just because someone offers money—that needs your permission, so the office should say no and check with the person in charge.

### Question 58

Even if someone works at the office, they still get to see their own medical information like any other patient—the office just checks it is really them first.

### Question 59

The rule works both ways: just as the office shares only what is needed, it should also ask for only what it needs instead of requesting everything.

### Question 60

When the law says to report something, the office reports it—the 'minimum' rule does not get in the way of following the law.

### Question 61

If another doctor's office says 'we only need these two pages to bill the insurance,' the office can trust them and send those two pages.

### Question 62

The government's rule-checkers get to see what they need to do their job, and the office must show them.

### Question 63

If you ask a trusted helper to handle your paperwork for you, that helper gets to see your information just like you would.

### Question 64

When the law requires sharing information, it goes in the 'allowed and exempt from the minimum rule' pile.

### Question 65

A permission form is like a signed note that says exactly what can be shared and why—it is written down, specific, and does not last forever.

### Question 66

One rule, two situations: your own record is fully yours to see, but the office still trims down what it sends to the insurance company to only what is needed for billing.

### Question 67

You would not tell a friend your sibling's secrets without permission. The office should not share a patient's information with family unless the patient has given permission.

### Question 68

When mailing a letter, you put it in the right envelope and check the address. Faxing patient information is similar: send only what is needed and make sure it goes to the right number.

### Question 69

A new worker gets the key to their own locker, not the key to every locker in the building. Access grows only as the job needs it.

### Question 70

Treatment is everything the care team does together to help a patient get better—including doctors coordinating with each other.

### Question 71

Before your first day at a new school, your old school sends just the records the new school needs—not every single paper from years past.

### Question 72

An insurance plan checking quality for its own members is allowed to ask for their information, because the members already have a relationship with that plan.

### Question 73

A tiny shop and a huge store both lock up at night, but they do it in ways that fit their size. The privacy rule works the same way—everyone protects information, scaled to their situation.

### Question 74

A doctor's office should not hand over a list of who takes which medicine to a salesperson—that is private, and sharing it needs the patient's permission.

### Question 75

When you switch to a new doctor, the office sends the notes the new doctor needs to keep helping you—the office handles the transfer so you do not have to carry papers yourself.

### Question 76

Billing your insurance does not need a signed form, but the office still protects your information and only uses what it needs for the bill.

### Question 77

Two ideas working together: share only what you need to share, and keep what you do share safe—like taking only the money you need from the bank and carrying it in a locked pouch.

### Question 78

If the insurance company asks for proof that a service was needed, the office sends just the papers that prove it—not your whole file.

### Question 79

Some rules are true and some are not. The false idea here is that you need a signed form before doctors can share information to treat you—you do not.

### Question 80

If you accidentally mail a letter to the wrong house, you tell an adult in charge so it can be fixed. The office does the same when a record goes to the wrong place.

### Question 81

To share information with another office to help that office run, the patient must be connected to both offices, and the information must be about that connection.

### Question 82

If a trusted official says 'I only need these two items for my job,' the office can trust that and provide those two items.

### Question 83

The rule is about balance: share enough to get the job done, but not a drop more than needed.

### Question 84

Just like a store sends the bill to your insurance so it can get paid, the doctor's office does the same—and it only sends the details needed for the bill.

### Question 85

The best answer is the one that shares the right amount with the right person: sending the specialist only the recent results they need, without making the patient fill out extra forms.
